newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's bid to lengthen maturities inches forward.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's bid to lengthen maturities inches forward.

text.p: Brazil's struggle to extend the average maturity on its massive stock of internal debt has been frustratingly slow over the past two years and analysts say the effort promises to remain an uphill battle.

"Despite the fall in inflation, the authorities have not managed to extend the maturity profile of (much of) their growing local debt," said Marcelo Carvalho, chief economist at J.P. Morgan in Brazil.

Maturities on weekly issues of Central Bank bonds have lengthened to 56 days from 35 days over the past two years. But the average maturity on National Treasury paper is about four months, virtually unchanged since the government launched its anti-inflation plan in July 1994.
Lengthening maturities would improve Brazil's risk profile by giving the Central Bank and the Treasury more breathing space in rolling over the nation's mammoth stock of internal debt.
Currently, the two institutions roll over some 127 billion reais ($124.2 billion) in bonds every four months.

In August, the Treasury began issuing fixed-rate 12-month paper to help extend average maturity periods. But it has done so tentatively, issuing just 1.4 billion reais of 12-month paper over the past two months.
By comparison, nearly 15 billion reais of six-month paper was issued in the same period.
Economists say the government is reluctant to step up issuance of 12-month bonds partly because it fears rejection by the market.

"The government can't put a lot of longer-term paper on the market out of caution," said Matthew Taylor, an economist at the Sao Paulo-based consulting firm Trend. "They don't want to get stuck in a situation where they put it out and the market doesn't eat it up."

Investor focus on short-term paper is primarily due to Brazil's unusually high interest rates -- hiked 18 months ago to attract dollar flows after Mexico's peso crisis -- which have distorted domestic bond pricing.

Unlike in most developing countries, where longer-term bonds usually pay higher yields than shorter-term paper, the opposite is the case in Brazil. This is mostly due to expectations of steady declines in monthly interest rates, which have fallen from about 4 percent in April 1995 to about 1.8 percent today.

Such an environment limits demand for long-term paper as short-term paper yields more and is less risky. In addition, currency risk mitigates the advantages of locking in high long-term yields in an environment of falling rates.
It also tempers the government's desire to issue longer paper for fear of getting stuck with too much expensive fixed-rate paper, economists said.

"I think the government has decided it will not issue securities with a higher maturity (than 12 months) unless they have floating rates or call options," said an economist at a large U.S. bank in Brazil who requested anonymity.

News reports this week said the Treasury was so concerned about the consequences of declining interest rates on its long-term debt stock that it was considering slowing down the issuance of 12-month, fixed-rate paper.
A Treasury official declined to comment on the report.
While some economists agreed that the Treasury might soon be tempted to issue a floating rate instrument or one that had a call option, they said the idea would not sit well with the Central Bank.

"If the government wants to create confidence in its currency, it does so by issuing long-term fixed rate paper. That may be more expensive, but this is more than just a question of money," said Dany Rappaport, chief economist at MCM Consultores in Brazil.
Rappaport said the Treasury would not slow issuance of 12-month paper, but he added that issues would remain relatively small throughout 1996.
-- Sao Paulo newsroom, 5511 232-4411
